title: Defensive Tracking Footwork
primarySkill: Defensive tracking footwork
objective: Develop the balanced footwork required to track a moving opponent while remaining able to react safely to changes of direction.
groundSize: Multiple lanes measuring approximately 8 metres long and 3 metres wide.
coachingDifficulty: 1 – Simple organisation and observation
setup:
Construct parallel lanes approximately 8 metres long and 3 metres wide.
Place one attacker and one defender at the beginning of each lane.
The attacker begins approximately 1.5 metres in front of the defender and faces the same direction.
Mark a finishing line at the end of each lane.
Ensure neighbouring lanes are separated sufficiently to prevent collisions.
Players work in pairs and alternate attacking and defending roles.
howTheDrillWorks:
On the coach’s signal, the attacker moves forward through the lane at approximately 50 per cent speed.
The attacker may change pace and move laterally but must remain inside the lane.
The defender tracks the attacker without making contact, attempting to remain approximately one arm’s length away.
The defender keeps their body square enough to respond in either direction and avoids crossing their feet.
The attacker continues until reaching the finishing line.
The defender earns one point by remaining balanced and within one arm’s length when the attacker crosses the line.
Players walk back outside the lane, exchange roles and repeat.
Complete four to six repetitions in each role.
coachingPoints: Adopt a balanced stance with knees bent, chest upright and weight through the balls of the feet.
Use short, controlled steps rather than long strides when close to the attacker.
Keep the feet moving and avoid planting both feet during the attacker’s change of direction.
Watch the attacker’s hips and trunk rather than reacting only to the head or football.
Maintain enough space to react without allowing the attacker to accelerate freely.
Accelerate when the attacker moves away and shorten the steps when closing.
Avoid crossing the feet during lateral movement.
Keep the head upright to preserve vision and awareness.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether defenders maintain a stable athletic stance.
Whether defenders remain within an effective tracking distance.
Whether players can change direction without crossing their feet.
Whether defenders shorten their stride as they approach the attacker.
Whether players keep their head and eyes up throughout the movement.
Whether the attacker can change pace without the defender becoming upright or unbalanced.

commonErrors.error: Defender stands upright while tracking.
commonErrors.correction: Lower the hips, bend the knees and keep the chest over the feet.

commonErrors.error: Defender watches the attacker’s feet.
commonErrors.correction: Direct the defender’s eyes towards the hips and centre of mass.

commonErrors.error: Defender crosses their feet when moving sideways.
commonErrors.correction: Use short lateral adjustment steps and keep the feet underneath the body.

commonErrors.error: Defender moves too close and is beaten by one step.
commonErrors.correction: Maintain one arm’s length until the attacker’s movement becomes predictable.

commonErrors.error: Defender takes long strides near the attacker.
commonErrors.correction: Shorten the steps before entering tackling distance.

progressions: Allow the attacker to use sharper changes of direction and greater speed.
Introduce a football so the defender must track the ball carrier’s hips rather than follow the football.
Have the coach call a colour at the finishing end that the attacker must move towards.
Reduce the lane width to demand more precise defensive footwork.
regressions: Reduce the attacker to walking speed.
Allow only one pre-planned change of direction.
Increase the lane width and shorten the working distance.
Have the defender shadow the attacker from beside them rather than from behind.
successIndicators: Remain balanced during changes of direction.
Keep their feet active and underneath their body.
Track within an effective defensive distance.
React to the attacker’s hips rather than guessing.
matchApplication: Effective tackling begins before contact. Defenders must track an opponent’s movement, control the closing space and remain balanced enough to react when a ball carrier changes direction, accelerates or attempts to evade. This drill establishes the footwork required to contain an opponent before attempting a legal tackle.

title: Safe Contact Shape with Tackle Bags
primarySkill: Safe initial tackling contact
objective: Introduce a safe and repeatable body shape for legal tackling contact using stationary tackle bags before players tackle a partner.
groundSize: Contact stations approximately 5 metres long and 4 metres wide.
equipment: Optional mouthguards where required by club policy
coachingDifficulty: 2 – Basic coaching knowledge and one main teaching point
setup:
Create several contact stations with one tackle bag at each station.
A holder stands behind each bag in a stable position with feet staggered.
The tackler begins 2 metres in front of the bag.
A coach should be positioned where head placement and body alignment can be observed clearly.
Players rotate through tackler, bag holder and recovery roles.
Under 8 players should use soft shields, walking speed and shoulder placement only.
howTheDrillWorks:
The tackler begins in a balanced stance facing the tackle bag.
On the coach’s signal, the tackler takes two or three controlled steps towards the bag.
The player lowers their centre of gravity by bending through the knees and hips.
The tackler places the near shoulder into the lower half of the bag while keeping the head safely to one side.
The arms wrap around the bag immediately after shoulder contact.
The player takes two short driving steps while the bag holder provides light resistance.
The tackler stops on the coach’s call, maintains balance and releases.
Players reset before repeating from the opposite shoulder.
Complete three to five repetitions on each side before rotating.
coachingPoints: Make contact with the shoulder rather than the head or extended arms.
Keep the head upright and positioned safely to the side of the bag.
Contact below the shoulders and above the knees.
Bend through the knees and hips rather than folding at the waist.
Place the lead foot close enough to create a stable base.
Wrap both arms immediately after the shoulder makes contact.
Drive with short steps instead of launching or leaving the ground.
Stop and release immediately on the coach’s call.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the head remains to the side of the contact point.
Whether the shoulder contacts the legal target area.
Whether the tackler bends through the knees and hips.
Whether both arms wrap after contact.
Whether the feet continue moving without the player launching.
Whether players can perform the technique equally from both sides.

commonErrors.error: Tackler places the head in front of the bag.
commonErrors.correction: Move the head firmly to the side before shoulder contact.

commonErrors.error: Player reaches with the arms before making body contact.
commonErrors.correction: Step close, make shoulder contact and then wrap.

commonErrors.error: Tackler bends at the waist and drops the eyes.
commonErrors.correction: Lower through the knees and hips while keeping the chest and eyes up.

commonErrors.error: Player launches from too far away.
commonErrors.correction: Reduce the approach distance and place the lead foot closer to the bag.

commonErrors.error: Contact is too high.
commonErrors.correction: Aim the shoulder at the lower half of the bag within the legal tackling zone.

progressions: Allow the bag holder to move slowly forwards or sideways.
Add a football secured against the tackle bag to provide a visual target.
Increase the approach to 3–4 metres while preserving controlled speed.
Finish with the tackler holding the bag stable for two seconds before releasing.
regressions: Begin with stationary shoulder placement and no approach.
Remove the driving steps and rehearse only contact, wrap and release.
Use a lighter hand shield rather than a full tackle bag.
Have the coach physically guide the player’s head and shoulder position at walking speed.
successIndicators: Position the head safely to the side.
Contact with the shoulder inside the legal tackling zone.
Wrap both arms immediately after contact.
Maintain a stable base and active feet.
matchApplication: The drill introduces the body shape used when tackling an opponent from the front or side. Safe head placement, legal shoulder contact and immediate arm wrapping reduce the likelihood of high contact, missed tackles and unsafe collisions.

title: Fend-Off Control and Re-Entry
primarySkill: Maintaining tackle position against a controlled fend-off
objective: Develop the ability to absorb or avoid a controlled fend-off, maintain balance and re-enter the tackle without grabbing the opponent’s arm illegally or making high contact.
groundSize: Channels approximately 7 metres long and 4 metres wide.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations and several observable behaviours
setup:
Create several 7-metre channels.
The ball carrier begins with the football approximately 3 metres from the defender.
The ball carrier may present one open hand as a controlled fend-off.
The fend-off must contact only the tackler’s upper chest or shoulder and may not contact the face, throat or head.
The defender may deflect the arm, move their head and body line, or recover after initial separation.
A third player observes safety and technique.
Tackles remain upright.
howTheDrillWorks:
The ball carrier moves towards the defender at approximately 50 per cent speed.
The defender closes space and prepares to tackle.
The attacker presents one controlled fend-off with an open hand.
The defender keeps the chin clear, protects the head and avoids leaning into the extended arm.
The defender may use the near forearm to guide the fend away without striking or grabbing.
The defender maintains active feet and moves back towards the attacker’s torso.
Once past the fend, the defender makes legal shoulder contact and wraps both arms.
The tackler controls the opponent upright for one second.
The coach calls “release”.
Players rotate roles after two repetitions on each side.
coachingPoints: Keep the eyes open and head upright when the fend is presented.
Avoid leading with the face or throat.
Do not grab, wrench or pull the extended arm.
Use footwork and body angle to move inside or around the fend.
Guide the arm away with an open forearm or hand where appropriate.
Re-establish close body position before attempting the wrap.
Keep the final contact below the shoulders and above the knees.
Maintain control without lifting or rotating the opponent.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the fend-off remains controlled and below the tackler’s neck.
Whether defenders avoid direct facial contact.
Whether players remain balanced after separation.
Whether the defender uses footwork rather than arm wrestling.
Whether re-entry occurs through the legal tackle zone.
Whether the tackle remains upright and controlled.

commonErrors.error: Tackler leads with the face into the fend.
commonErrors.correction: Move the head off-line and approach with the shoulder.

commonErrors.error: Defender grabs and pulls the extended arm.
commonErrors.correction: Guide the arm away and continue moving towards the torso.

commonErrors.error: Tackler stops their feet after the fend.
commonErrors.correction: Keep adjusting until close body position is restored.

commonErrors.error: Defender reaches from outside the fend.
commonErrors.correction: Move the feet past the extended arm before wrapping.

commonErrors.error: Ball carrier fends towards the face or neck.
commonErrors.correction: Stop the drill and reset the fend to the upper chest or shoulder only.

progressions: Allow the ball carrier to choose which arm presents the fend.
Increase the ball carrier’s speed slightly.
Allow the defender to choose whether to deflect, evade or absorb the fend.
Permit the ball carrier to attempt a handball after the fend.
regressions: Practise fend avoidance without completing a tackle.
Use a soft pad instead of a player’s hand.
successIndicators: Protect the head and neck from the fend.
Avoid grabbing or wrenching the opponent’s arm.
Continue moving the feet after initial separation.
Re-enter through the legal tackle zone.
matchApplication: Ball carriers frequently use a fend-off to prevent or break tackles. Defenders must protect themselves, remain balanced and continue working towards the opponent’s torso rather than reaching, grabbing the arm or making desperate high contact.

title: Deceptive Ball-Carrier Pressure
primarySkill: Defending against deception before tackling
objective: Develop the ability to remain balanced against ball, handball and kick fakes before committing to a legal tackle.
groundSize: Contest areas approximately 10 metres by 8 metres.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Mark multiple contest areas with one exit gate and two disposal targets.
Position one ball carrier and one defender approximately 3 metres apart.
A third player acts as observer and one of the disposal targets.
The attacker may use a handball fake, kick fake, shoulder baulk or football transfer.
The attacker may use no more than two deceptive actions.
The defender must remain balanced and protect the scoring gate.
All tackles remain controlled and upright.
howTheDrillWorks:
On the observer’s signal, the attacker begins moving towards the exit gate.
The attacker may use up to two deceptive actions.
The defender closes space without committing to the first ball movement.
The defender tracks the attacker’s hips and supporting foot position.
If the attacker attempts a real disposal, the defender applies legal pressure without making late contact.
If the attacker retains possession and enters tackle range, the defender completes a legal tackle.
The defender scores two points for a completed tackle and one point for forcing an ineffective disposal.
The attacker scores one point for a clean disposal or controlled gate entry.
Players exchange roles after each repetition.
Complete five to seven repetitions per player.
coachingPoints: Read the hips, trunk and supporting foot rather than only the football.
Maintain active feet through every fake.
Avoid leaving the ground or reaching towards a kick fake.
Preserve a reaction buffer until the attacker commits.
Recognise the difference between disposal preparation and actual release.
Close the near foot before completing the tackle.
Control the torso and disposal arm rather than grabbing the football.
Avoid late contact after a completed disposal.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether defenders react to body movement or only football movement.
Whether players remain balanced through repeated fakes.
Whether the scoring gate remains protected.
Whether defenders identify actual disposal release.
Whether the tackle is attempted from close range.
Whether late contact is avoided.
Whether attackers use realistic deception.

commonErrors.error: Defender reaches towards a handball fake.
commonErrors.correction: Keep the hands ready and continue moving the feet.

commonErrors.error: Player jumps at a kick fake.
commonErrors.correction: Stay grounded and read the supporting leg and hips.

commonErrors.error: Defender waits too long after the attacker commits.
commonErrors.correction: Reaccelerate as soon as the movement becomes genuine.

commonErrors.error: Tackler focuses on the football and concedes the exit gate.
commonErrors.correction: Protect the dangerous running line first.

commonErrors.error: Defender makes contact after a clean disposal.
commonErrors.correction: Stop the pressure action once release is complete.

commonErrors.error: Attacker performs unrealistic repeated fakes.
commonErrors.correction: Limit deception to two match-like movements.

progressions: Allow unrestricted deceptive actions within a five-second limit.
Add a support receiver who may move.
Permit the attacker to use a controlled fend-off.
Increase the contest area and approach speed.
Add a second defender arriving late.
successIndicators: Recognise genuine disposal or movement commitment.
Complete legal tackles from close range.
matchApplication: Advanced ball carriers use fakes to make defenders stop, jump or reach. Effective tacklers remain disciplined, continue moving and commit only when the opponent’s movement or disposal becomes genuine.

title: Last-Line Goal-Saving Tackle
primarySkill: Completing a goal-saving tackle as the last defender
objective: Develop the composure and positioning required for a last defender to delay the ball carrier, protect the goal line and complete a legal goal-saving tackle.
groundSize: A forward area approximately 25 metres from goal and the width of the goal square.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Position an attacker with the football 20–25 metres from goal.
Place the last defender 4–6 metres goal side and slightly inside.
Position a feeder outside the area.
Mark one boundary-side escape lane.
A fourth player acts as observer and rebound target.
The attacker may run towards goal, attempt a shot or move towards the boundary.
The defender must protect the direct path to goal.
Tackles remain controlled and upright unless safe ground contact has been formally introduced.
howTheDrillWorks:
The feeder releases the attacker into the scoring area.
The defender retreats or adjusts while remaining between the attacker and goal.
The defender closes the direct shooting line.
If the attacker remains outside tackle range, the defender corrals towards the boundary side.
If the attacker prepares to shoot, the defender closes the disposal window.
When safe contact range develops, the defender completes a legal tackle.
The attacker scores two points for a goal and one point for reaching the goal square under control.
The defender scores two points for a tackle and one point for forcing a wide or rushed shot.
If the defender wins possession, they dispose to the rebound target.
Players rotate through attacker, defender, feeder and target roles.
coachingPoints: Remain goal side and protect the direct scoring line.
Avoid charging too early and allowing the attacker to run around the defender.
Use the boundary side as the lower-risk escape.
Read whether the attacker intends to run, evade or shoot.
Close quickly as the ball becomes exposed for a shot.
Avoid contact with an extended kicking leg.
Complete the tackle from a balanced side-on position.
Secure possession and exit safely after winning the football.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the defender remains between the attacker and goal.
Whether direct scoring space is protected.
Whether the attacker is influenced towards the boundary.
Whether the defender recognises the shot preparation.
Whether contact avoids the kicking leg.
Whether the tackle occurs from balance.
Whether the defender completes a safe rebound disposal.

commonErrors.error: Defender charges and is evaded.
commonErrors.correction: Delay and maintain goal-side position until the attacker commits.

commonErrors.error: Player protects the boundary and concedes the direct goal line.
commonErrors.correction: Prioritise the shortest path to goal.

commonErrors.error: Defender attempts contact from too far away.
commonErrors.correction: Corral until the near foot can arrive close.

commonErrors.error: Tackler dives across the kicking leg.
commonErrors.correction: Close the torso from the side and use smother pressure if the kick is committed.

commonErrors.error: Defender wins possession but turns it over centrally.
commonErrors.correction: Use the safest rebound target.

commonErrors.error: Player becomes passive near goal.
commonErrors.correction: Continue reducing space while preserving balance.

progressions: Add an attacking support runner.
Add a recovering defender.
Allow the attacker unrestricted shot and handball choices.
Begin from a turnover with both players moving.
Introduce scoreboard and late-game context.
regressions: Use a scoring gate instead of goals.
Begin the defender closer to the attacker.
successIndicators: Influence the attacker towards lower-value space.
Complete a legal goal-saving tackle or force a rushed shot.
matchApplication: Last-line defenders must balance urgency with patience. Protecting the goal, delaying the attacker and tackling at the correct moment can prevent a certain score without conceding a free kick or being eliminated by an early commitment.

title: Interchange-Side Pressure Communication
primarySkill: Maintaining pressure near the interchange area
objective: Develop clear defensive communication and opponent handover when players enter or leave the field near the interchange side.
groundSize: A wing channel approximately 40 metres long and 22 metres wide, including a marked interchange zone.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Mark a wing channel beside a designated interchange area.
Divide players into attacking and defending teams.
Place one substitute player from each team inside the interchange zone.
The coach controls when players exchange.
Mark one forward gate and one boundary release gate.
The attacking team begins with possession.
Defenders must maintain pressure while identifying players entering and leaving the field.
Tackles remain controlled and legal.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team begins moving the football along the wing.
Defenders establish inside position and protect the forward gate.
The coach calls an interchange for one or both teams.
Players leaving the field move towards the interchange zone.
Incoming players enter and immediately take up an attacking or defensive role.
Defenders communicate opponent handovers involving the outgoing and incoming players.
The nearest balanced defender continues direct pressure on the ball carrier.
Supporting defenders protect the corridor and new receiver options.
Attackers score one point for entering the forward gate.
Defenders score two points for a tackle or turnover and one point for forcing a boundary stoppage.
Reset after a score, turnover or completed interchange sequence.
coachingPoints: Maintain focus on the live football during interchange movement.
Clearly identify which player is leaving and which player is entering.
Communicate opponent handovers before the incoming player becomes free.
Do not follow an outgoing opponent beyond the playing area.
Preserve inside and corridor position.
The nearest balanced defender continues pressuring the football.
Incoming defenders must scan before joining pressure.
Avoid congestion around the interchange line.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether players recognise interchange movement.
Whether outgoing opponents are released appropriately.
Whether incoming players are identified.
Whether opponent handovers are communicated.
Whether the live ball remains pressured.
Whether central space remains protected.
Whether players avoid crowding the interchange area.

commonErrors.error: Defender follows an opponent towards or beyond the interchange line.
commonErrors.correction: Hand the player over and return attention to the live field.

commonErrors.error: Incoming attacker enters unopposed.
commonErrors.correction: Identify and communicate the new receiver before entry.

commonErrors.error: Incoming defender runs directly at the football.
commonErrors.correction: Scan opponents and team structure before applying pressure.

commonErrors.error: Defenders lose inside position during the interchange.
commonErrors.correction: Preserve corridor protection while roles change.

commonErrors.error: Players crowd the interchange gate.
commonErrors.correction: Maintain clear entry and exit lanes.

commonErrors.error: Pressure stops while players communicate.
commonErrors.correction: Keep one defender actively pressuring the ball carrier.

progressions: Conduct simultaneous interchanges.
Allow the incoming attacker to become an immediate receiver.
Add a switch-of-play option.
Continue into full-ground transition.
Remove the coach’s interchange warning.
regressions: Interchange one player at a time.
Pause briefly during the first rehearsals.
Use pressure touches instead of tackles.
Reduce the channel width and player numbers.
successIndicators: Maintain pressure on the live football.
Complete safe tackles near the boundary.
matchApplication: Interchange movement can create temporary confusion and unmarked players. Clear communication allows teams to maintain pressure and defensive structure while personnel changes occur beside live play.

title: Spoil-to-Tackle Pressure
primarySkill: Applying immediate tackle pressure after an aerial spoil
objective: Teach defenders to transition from an aerial spoil into organised ground-level pressure on the player who collects the loose football.
groundSize: Contest areas approximately 18 metres by 16 metres.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Position one attacker and one defender for a controlled aerial contest.
Place two ground-level players from each team around the contest.
Position a kicker 18–25 metres away.
Mark two disposal targets outside the contest area.
The defender’s initial aim is to spoil safely.
Ground-level players compete after the football reaches the ground.
Full tackling begins once a player gains possession and reaches safe contact height.
howTheDrillWorks:
The kicker delivers the football to the aerial contest.
The aerial defender attempts a controlled spoil towards a designated safe area.
Ground-level players read the football’s drop.
The nearest player attempts to gain possession.
Defenders identify the ball winner immediately.
The nearest balanced defender closes and applies legal tackle pressure.
Other defenders protect the nearest disposal targets.
If the football remains loose, players continue competing safely.
The possession team scores one point for a clean disposal to a target.
Defenders score two points for a tackle or turnover and one point for forcing an ineffective disposal.
Rotate aerial and ground-level roles.
coachingPoints: Spoil away from the most dangerous attacking space where possible.
Land safely and regain balance before re-entering play.
Ground-level defenders should position front and square.
Identify the player who wins possession.
Avoid tackling while the player’s head remains over the football.
Close the disposal side as the collector rises.
Supporting defenders protect the outlet options.
Release immediately if the football spills.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the spoil is controlled and directed.
Whether aerial players land safely.
Whether ground-level defenders hold useful positions.
Whether the possession winner is identified quickly.
Whether contact is delayed until safe tackling height.
Whether outlet targets are covered.
Whether defenders react correctly to another spill.

commonErrors.error: Spoil is directed into dangerous central space.
commonErrors.correction: Aim towards the boundary or supporting defenders where possible.

commonErrors.error: Aerial defender falls into the ground contest.
commonErrors.correction: Land, regain balance and then re-enter.

commonErrors.error: Ground players stand behind the aerial contest.
commonErrors.correction: Establish front-and-square positions.

commonErrors.error: Defender tackles while the collector’s head is down.
commonErrors.correction: Control the exit and wait until the player rises.

commonErrors.error: All defenders attack the collector.
commonErrors.correction: Keep one pressure player and protect outlets with others.

commonErrors.error: Tackler continues holding after another spill.
commonErrors.correction: Release immediately and contest the football.

progressions: Allow the attacker to mark if the spoil is ineffective.
Add a second aerial attacker.
Continue live play after the first disposal.
Vary the kick’s height and direction.
Introduce a scoring target near goal.
regressions: Use a coach-directed spoil or ball drop.
Reduce the number of ground-level players.
successIndicators: Apply legal pressure at safe height.
Create tackles, turnovers or ineffective disposals.
matchApplication: A spoil is only the first defensive action. Teams must organise immediately at ground level to prevent the opposition collecting and exiting cleanly after the aerial contest.

title: Press Recovery After Kick Over the Top
Shepherd-Release Defensive Handover
primarySkill: Maintaining pressure when a ball carrier is protected by a shepherd
objective: Teach defenders to avoid illegal contact through a shepherd, communicate a defensive handover and continue pressure on the ball carrier from a safe angle.
groundSize: Lanes approximately 18 metres long and 10 metres wide.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Position one ball carrier and one supporting attacker at one end of the lane.
Place two defenders between the attackers and the scoring line.
The supporting attacker may provide a legal controlled shepherd.
The shepherd must remain within legal distance and may not make high or forceful contact.
Defenders must communicate whether to fight around, switch or hand over.
A feeder and observer stand outside the lane.
Tackles remain controlled and upright.
howTheDrillWorks:
The feeder starts the ball carrier with a handball.
The supporting attacker moves into a legal shepherding position.
The nearest defender reads the shepherd and chooses a safe route around it.
The second defender communicates whether to switch onto the ball carrier.
If the first defender is delayed, the second defender becomes the primary pressure player.
The released defender recovers to the supporting attacker or next disposal option.
The nearest balanced defender completes a legal tackle when safe range develops.
Attackers score one point for crossing the scoring line.
Defenders score two points for a tackle or turnover and one point for forcing a backwards disposal.
Rotate all roles after each repetition.
coachingPoints: Recognise the shepherd before entering contact.
Avoid charging directly through the supporting player.
Communicate whether to stay, switch or hand over.
The defender with the clearest path pressures the ball carrier.
The delayed defender recovers to the support attacker.
Maintain vision of the ball carrier while navigating the shepherd.
Re-establish balance before tackling.
Keep all shepherd and tackle contact legal and controlled.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether defenders identify the shepherd early.
Whether direct collision with the shepherd is avoided.
Whether communication occurs before the ball carrier escapes.
Whether responsibility transfers cleanly.
Whether the delayed defender recovers to a useful opponent.
Whether the tackle is completed from balance.
Whether the shepherd remains legal.

commonErrors.error: Defender runs directly into the shepherd.
commonErrors.correction: Move around the body and communicate a handover.

commonErrors.error: Both defenders attack the ball carrier.
commonErrors.correction: Allocate one pressure defender and one support-opponent defender.

commonErrors.error: Delayed defender stops after being blocked.
commonErrors.correction: Recover to the shepherd or next receiver.

commonErrors.error: Switch call occurs too late.
commonErrors.correction: Communicate as soon as the shepherding line develops.

commonErrors.error: Tackler arrives off balance after changing route.
commonErrors.correction: Use adjustment steps before contact.

commonErrors.error: Shepherd contacts high or moves outside legal position.
commonErrors.correction: Reduce speed and reinforce legal shepherding technique.

progressions: Allow the shepherd to change sides.
Add a second support attacker.
Remove predetermined defender roles.
Continue play after the first disposal.
Introduce a boundary-side shepherd scenario.
regressions: Walk through the shepherd and switch pattern.
Predetermine which defender takes the ball carrier.
successIndicators: Maintain pressure on the ball carrier.
Complete legal tackles from balanced positions.
matchApplication: Shepherds are used to create space for ball carriers. Defenders must communicate and transfer responsibility rather than allowing one block to remove all pressure from the possession chain.

title: On-Field Pressure Leadership Calls
primarySkill: Organising team pressure through player-led communication
objective: Develop on-field leaders who can identify the pressure situation, assign defensive roles and organise teammates without relying on coach instructions.
groundSize: A grid approximately 35 metres long and 28 metres wide with central and outside scoring gates.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Divide players into an attacking possession team and a defending pressure team.
Nominate one defensive leader for each repetition.
Mark one central scoring gate and two outside gates.
The attacking team begins with possession at one end.
The coach varies attacking numbers, starting positions and available space.
The defensive leader must organise the press before and during play.
Coaches remain silent during each live repetition.
Rotate the leadership role every two to three repetitions.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team begins moving the football towards the scoring gates.
The defensive leader identifies the immediate threat.
The leader calls who pressures the ball carrier.
The leader assigns supporting defenders to central space and nearby receivers.
Defenders adjust their positions according to the call.
Pressure responsibility rotates after each disposal.
The leader continues communicating switches, holds, recoveries and pressing triggers.
Legal tackles are permitted when safe contact range develops.
Attackers score two points through the central gate and one point through an outside gate.
Defenders score two points for a tackle or turnover and one point for forcing a backwards disposal.
After each repetition, teammates rate the clarity and timing of the leadership calls.
coachingPoints: Identify the greatest attacking threat first.
Use short, consistent and specific calls.
Assign one direct pressure player.
Protect the corridor and next receiver.
Communicate before teammates need to act.
Continue organising after the first disposal.
Adjust the call when the situation changes.
Leaders should direct rather than chase every contest themselves.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the leader scans before communicating.
Whether calls identify specific players or spaces.
Whether teammates respond immediately.
Whether pressure roles remain clear after disposals.
Whether central space stays protected.
Whether the leader adapts when the initial plan breaks down.
Whether communication improves team tackling opportunities.

commonErrors.error: Leader gives several conflicting instructions.
commonErrors.correction: Use one priority call at a time.

commonErrors.error: Calls occur after the receiver gains possession.
commonErrors.correction: Communicate while the football is travelling.

commonErrors.error: Leader follows the football and loses awareness.
commonErrors.correction: Maintain a position that allows scanning of the full structure.

commonErrors.error: Pressure player is not identified.
commonErrors.correction: Name or point to the nearest balanced defender.

commonErrors.error: Teammates ignore the call.
commonErrors.correction: Establish common team language and require verbal acknowledgement.

commonErrors.error: Leader stops communicating after the first contest.
commonErrors.correction: Continue organising until possession is secured or play ends.

progressions: Remove the nominated leader and require leadership to emerge naturally.
Add scoreboard and time-pressure scenarios.
Change attacking numbers during live play.
Allow the attacking team unrestricted kicks and switches.
Require different players to lead each field zone.
regressions: Give the leader several seconds to organise before play begins.
Allow the coach to prompt the first leadership call.
matchApplication: Pressure systems fail when players wait for coaches to organise them. On-field leaders must identify threats, allocate roles and maintain defensive connection throughout live play.

title: Forward-50 Chase-Down Tackle
primarySkill: Completing a chase-down tackle inside attacking 50
objective: Develop the ability to chase an opponent exiting defensive 50, reach a safe side-on position and complete a legal tackle that creates a scoring opportunity.
groundSize: A lane approximately 25 metres long and 10 metres wide inside attacking 50.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Position a defender with the football near the goal line or defensive pocket.
Place a chasing forward 3–5 metres behind and slightly inside.
Position an exit receiver near the end of the lane.
Place an attacking scoring target in front of goal.
A feeder or observer manages each repetition.
The ball carrier attempts to exit or dispose to the receiver.
The chaser must remain clear of direct contact through the opponent’s back.
Match players appropriately for speed and physical capacity.
howTheDrillWorks:
The ball carrier begins accelerating towards the exit receiver.
The chasing forward accelerates towards the opponent’s inside or outside hip.
The chaser attempts to close before the ball carrier reaches disposal range.
The defender may change pace once.
The chaser moves beside the ball carrier and decelerates.
A legal shoulder-and-wrap tackle is completed if safe range develops.
If the defender disposes, the chaser avoids late contact and continues towards the receiver.
The chaser scores two points for a tackle and one point for forcing an ineffective disposal.
If the forward wins possession, they have five seconds to attempt a score.
Rotate chaser, ball carrier, receiver and feeder roles.
coachingPoints: Sprint towards the ball carrier’s hip rather than directly at the spine.
Use the shortest legal pursuit angle.
Reduce the speed difference before contact.
Move beside the opponent before tackling.
Read the ball carrier’s disposal preparation.
Avoid contact after a clean kick or handball.
Continue pressure to the receiver if the disposal escapes.
Convert turnovers into a quick scoring attempt.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the chaser selects an effective angle.
Whether the defender’s speed is matched.
Whether contact occurs from the side.
Whether tackles remain above the knees and below the shoulders.
Whether late contact is avoided.
Whether the chaser continues to the next receiver.
Whether turnovers are converted into scoring opportunities.

commonErrors.error: Chaser runs directly into the opponent’s back.
commonErrors.correction: Pursue the hip and reach the side before contact.

commonErrors.error: Player reaches with one arm.
commonErrors.correction: Continue running until a two-arm wrap is available.

commonErrors.error: Tackler arrives at excessive speed.
commonErrors.correction: Shorten the final steps and match pace.

commonErrors.error: Chaser makes contact after disposal.
commonErrors.correction: Pull out and continue pressure towards the receiver.

commonErrors.error: Player stops after forcing a poor disposal.
commonErrors.correction: Continue to the next contest.

commonErrors.error: Turnover is followed by a rushed shot.
commonErrors.correction: Secure possession and select the highest-value scoring option.

progressions: Add an overlap exit runner.
Allow the ball carrier unrestricted changes of pace.
Begin the chaser farther behind.
Continue into a two-versus-two forward-pressure contest.
Introduce match-like ground contact for prepared players.
regressions: Begin the chaser level with the opponent’s hip.
Reduce both players to jogging speed.
Replace the tackle with a pressure touch.
matchApplication: Forward chase-down tackles can create high-value turnovers close to goal. Successful forwards combine maximum running effort with enough control to avoid dangerous contact or late free kicks.

title: Defensive Line Squeeze After Mark
primarySkill: Compressing defensive space after an opposition mark
objective: Teach a defensive unit to use the time created by an opposition mark to move forward, reduce receiver space and prepare coordinated pressure on the next possession.
groundSize: A grid approximately 35 metres long and 28 metres wide.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Position an attacking team across the grid.
Position defenders goalside and inside their direct opponents.
Begin with a controlled kick resulting in a mark.
Mark the protected area around the player who marks.
Place one central and two outside scoring gates.
The defender on the mark remains legal.
Other defenders use the pause to squeeze space and reorganise.
The marker may hold, kick or play on.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking player completes the mark.
The direct defender establishes the legal mark position.
Supporting defenders move forward and inside towards likely receivers.
Deeper defenders protect the long central target.
Players communicate opponent handovers created by the squeeze.
If the marker plays on, the direct defender applies immediate pressure.
If the marker disposes, the nearest defender closes the receiver while the football travels.
Legal tackles are permitted after possession is established.
Attackers score two points for a central exit and one point for an outside exit.
Defenders score two points for a tackle or turnover and one point for forcing a long uncontrolled kick.
Reset after each completed phase.
coachingPoints: Respect the protected area.
Use the mark to reset and compress defensive space.
Move forward together rather than individually.
Position inside likely receivers.
Protect the long central target.
Communicate handovers during the squeeze.
Remain ready for immediate play on.
Avoid squeezing so far that a long kick travels over the entire line.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the defender on the mark remains legal.
Whether supporting defenders squeeze immediately.
Whether likely receivers lose space.
Whether the long target remains protected.
Whether handovers are communicated.
Whether play-on pressure is immediate.
Whether the receiving player is pressured during the football’s flight.

commonErrors.error: Defenders stand still after the mark.
commonErrors.correction: Use the pause to reset and move forward.

commonErrors.error: Player on the mark enters the protected area.
commonErrors.correction: Hold the legal mark position until play on.

commonErrors.error: Defenders squeeze individually and create gaps.
commonErrors.correction: Move the entire line together.

commonErrors.error: Long central target becomes free.
commonErrors.correction: Keep a deeper defender protecting the dangerous space.

commonErrors.error: Players squeeze too close to short receivers.
commonErrors.correction: Maintain enough distance to react to a long disposal.

commonErrors.error: Defenders relax and concede play on.
commonErrors.correction: Stay balanced and ready for immediate movement.

progressions: Allow the marker to fake play on.
Add crossing receivers.
Increase kick distance.
Continue play for multiple possessions.
Introduce scoreboard and late-game scenarios.
regressions: Pause after the mark to position defenders.
Use handball only after the mark.
successIndicators: Respect the mark and protected area.
Squeeze space as a connected line.
Create pressure on the next possession.
matchApplication: An opposition mark gives defenders time to reorganise. Teams that squeeze forward together can remove easy receivers, force longer disposals and create tackle opportunities on the next possession.

title: Boundary Throw-In Pressure Trap
primarySkill: Creating pressure from a boundary throw-in
objective: Develop coordinated pressure that prevents a clean boundary-stoppage exit and traps possession against the line.
groundSize: A boundary area approximately 25 metres long and 18 metres wide.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Use an existing boundary line or mark one side of the grid as the boundary.
Position two rucks and matched midfielders near the throw-in point.
Place outside receivers inside and behind the stoppage.
Mark a dangerous central exit gate and a lower-value boundary gate.
A coach performs controlled boundary throw-ins.
Defenders begin inside their direct opponents.
Full tackling begins once possession is established.
Rotate players through inside, outside and ruck roles.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach throws the football in from the boundary.
Rucks compete to direct the football.
Midfielders contest the first possession.
The nearest defender pressures the ball carrier.
Supporting defenders protect the central exit and likely handball receiver.
Defenders attempt to keep possession near the boundary.
Legal tackles may be completed once safe contact range develops.
The possession team scores two points for a central exit and one point for a boundary exit.
Defenders score two points for a tackle or turnover and one point for forcing another boundary stoppage.
If the football exits the immediate area, play continues for one disposal.
Reset and change the throw-in depth or player alignment.
coachingPoints: Protect the inside and central exit.
Position inside direct opponents.
Identify the likely first receiver.
The nearest balanced defender pressures the football.
Supporting defenders close the inside handball and backwards release.
Use the boundary as part of the defensive trap.
Avoid overcommitting into the ruck contest.
Maintain legal tackle height as players emerge.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether defenders maintain inside position.
Whether central space is protected.
Whether the first ball carrier is pressured.
Whether likely receivers are covered.
Whether defenders keep the football near the boundary.
Whether tackles remain controlled in congestion.
Whether another stoppage is created.

commonErrors.error: Defenders stand boundary side of opponents.
commonErrors.correction: Reposition inside and protect the central exit.

commonErrors.error: Several defenders attack the ruck contest.
commonErrors.correction: Maintain outside and receiver coverage.

commonErrors.error: First possession escapes without pressure.
commonErrors.correction: Identify the likely receiver before the throw-in.

commonErrors.error: Backwards handball remains available.
commonErrors.correction: Position a support defender behind the immediate contest.

commonErrors.error: Tackler arrives high from congestion.
commonErrors.correction: Lower through the hips and approach the torso.

commonErrors.error: Defenders force play inside rather than towards the line.
commonErrors.correction: Use body angle to maintain the boundary trap.

progressions: Allow unrestricted ruck plans.
Add a forward target beyond the stoppage.
Continue live play after the first exit.
Introduce late-game boundary scenarios.
Add a second consecutive throw-in after a forced stoppage.
regressions: Use a coach handball from the boundary.
successIndicators: Use the boundary to restrict space.
matchApplication: Boundary stoppages provide an opportunity to trap possession against the line. Strong inside positioning and first-possession pressure can prevent dangerous central clearances.

title: Pressure Leadership and Tactical Assessment
primarySkill: Assessment of player-led tactical pressure
objective: Assess whether players can lead, organise and execute advanced pressure systems across tactical patterns, stoppages, transitions and match-like play.
groundSize: Full oval divided into five tactical assessment areas.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Construct five tactical assessment areas or phases.
Area 1 assesses player-led pressure organisation.
Area 2 assesses recognition of opposition exit patterns.
Area 3 assesses ruck-tap, boundary and secondary-stoppage pressure.
Area 4 assesses forward chase-down and intercept counter-pressure.
Area 5 assesses match-like pressure KPIs and leadership.
Nominate different leaders for each phase.
Assign coaches or observers to record performance.
Use one consistent scoring system across all areas.
Contact is match-like only for appropriately prepared players.
howTheDrillWorks:
In Area 1, a nominated player organises team pressure without coach assistance.
Observers assess scanning, communication, role allocation and adaptation.
In Area 2, defenders identify and counter repeated attacking exit patterns.
Observers assess recognition, anticipation and structural discipline.
In Area 3, players pressure first possession across ruck taps and repeated stoppages.
Observers assess reset speed, exit protection and tackle timing.
In Area 4, players complete forward chase-down and intercept counter-pressure scenarios.
Observers assess pursuit angles, turnover reaction and scoring conversion.
In Area 5, teams complete a pressure KPI match game.
Observers assess effective pressure actions, leadership and team connection.
Each assessed behaviour receives:
2 points: Demonstrated consistently and independently.
1 point: Demonstrated inconsistently or after prompting.
0 points: Not demonstrated or performed unsafely.
Any illegal or uncontrolled contact stops the repetition immediately.
Coaches record one technical strength, one tactical priority, one leadership priority and one recommended development drill for every player.
coachingPoints: Players should organise pressure independently.
Communication must identify specific roles and threats.
Opposition patterns should be recognised without reckless guessing.
First possession must be pressured at stoppages.
Repeated stoppages require rapid role reset.
Chase-down tackles must become side-on before contact.
Intercept turnovers require immediate counter-pressure.
Pressure KPIs should reflect genuine influence on play.
Legal tackling standards remain mandatory at match intensity.
Turnovers should create controlled attacking opportunities.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether leaders scan and communicate clearly.
Whether teammates respond to player-led calls.
Whether opposition patterns are recognised.
Whether defenders preserve structure while adjusting.
Whether stoppage pressure resets rapidly.
Whether chase-down tackles remain legal.
Whether counter-pressure follows intercepts.
Whether effective pressure actions are repeated.
Whether match context influences decisions.
Whether players require coach intervention.
Whether tackling remains safe under fatigue.

commonErrors.error: Players wait for coach instructions.
commonErrors.correction: Require nominated leaders to organise each phase.

commonErrors.error: Leadership calls are vague.
commonErrors.correction: Name the pressure player, receiver or space specifically.

commonErrors.error: Defenders guess opposition patterns too early.
commonErrors.correction: Confirm the cue before adjusting structure.

commonErrors.error: Stoppage roles are not reset.
commonErrors.correction: Release, regain feet and identify opponents immediately.

commonErrors.error: Chasers tackle directly through the back.
commonErrors.correction: Reach the hip and move beside the ball carrier.

commonErrors.error: Players pause after an intercept.
commonErrors.correction: Transition immediately into counter-pressure.

commonErrors.error: KPI scoring encourages individual chasing.
commonErrors.correction: Reward supporting pressure and receiver denial.

commonErrors.error: Tackle quality deteriorates under fatigue.
commonErrors.correction: Reduce work duration and restore legal technique.

commonErrors.error: Turnovers are followed by rushed attacking decisions.
commonErrors.correction: Secure the first possession and select the best option.

progressions: Complete all five phases as one continuous full-ground simulation.
Remove nominated leaders and assess natural leadership.
Introduce opponent-specific tactical plans.
Add complex scoreboard and time scenarios.
Repeat under controlled match fatigue.
Use player-led review and KPI analysis.
regressions: Reduce contact from match-like to controlled.
Return players to TK-100 before repeating the complete assessment.
successIndicators: Preserve legal technique at match intensity.
matchApplication: Elite teams require players who can organise pressure, recognise opposition tactics and maintain safe tackling standards without constant coach direction. This assessment measures the transition from coached pressure systems to independent match execution.

title: Opposition Spare Counter-Pressure
primarySkill: Maintaining pressure against an opposition spare player
objective: Develop the ability to pressure the ball carrier while identifying and limiting the influence of an opposition spare without abandoning dangerous central space.
groundSize: A grid approximately 30 metres long and 24 metres wide with central and outside scoring gates.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
- Divide players into an attacking team and a defending team.
- Give the attacking team one additional player.
- Mark one central scoring gate and two outside gates.
- The spare attacker may move anywhere inside the grid.
- Defenders begin in a connected shape protecting central space.
- Nominate one defender as the pressure organiser.
- The attacking team may use handball and short kicks.
- Tackles remain controlled and legal.
howTheDrillWorks:
1. The attacking team begins with possession at one end.
2. The nearest balanced defender closes the ball carrier.
3. Supporting defenders identify direct opponents and the spare attacker.
4. Defenders protect the corridor and most dangerous receiver.
5. The pressure organiser communicates whether to hold shape, switch or leave the lowest-risk attacker.
6. The attacking team attempts to use the spare to progress through a scoring gate.
7. Defenders rotate pressure after every disposal.
8. A legal tackle may be completed when safe range develops.
9. Attackers score two points through the central gate and one point through an outside gate.
10. Defenders score two points for a tackle or turnover and one point for forcing three consecutive backwards or lateral disposals.
11. Reset after a score, turnover or stoppage.
coachingPoints: - Accept that every attacker cannot be defended equally.
- Protect the greatest scoring threat first.
- The nearest balanced defender pressures the ball carrier.
- Supporting defenders position between the football and dangerous receivers.
- Leave the lowest-value option rather than opening the corridor.
- Communicate who is responsible for the spare.
- Move while the football is travelling.
- Avoid charging at the spare and freeing a more dangerous player.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: - Whether defenders identify the spare early.
- Whether central space remains protected.
- Whether the correct attacker is temporarily left free.
- Whether direct pressure reaches the ball carrier.
- Whether defenders communicate switches and handovers.
- Whether the spare is forced into lower-value possession.
- Whether tackle opportunities are created without structural collapse.

commonErrors.error: Defenders attempt to cover every attacker equally.| Prioritise the corridor, scoring gate and most dangerous receiver.
commonErrors.correction: One defender chases the spare across the grid.| Hold structure and hand responsibility over when appropriate.

commonErrors.error: Ball pressure disappears while players discuss the spare.| Maintain one active pressure defender at all times.
commonErrors.correction: Defenders leave a central receiver free.| Concede the widest or least dangerous option instead.

commonErrors.error: Pressure unit shifts too late.| Move while the football is travelling.
commonErrors.correction: Tackler lunges because of the numerical disadvantage.| Corral and delay until a balanced tackle opportunity develops.

progressions: - Give the attacking team two spare players.
- Allow unrestricted kicking.
- Remove the nominated pressure organiser.
- Continue play after a turnover.
- Add scoreboard and time-pressure scenarios.
regressions: - Keep the spare player in one designated lane.
- Predetermine the first two attacking disposals.
matchApplication: Opposition teams often create a spare behind or around the football. Defenders must maintain pressure without destroying their structure by chasing every available player.

title: Tackle-to-Spread Transition
primarySkill: Transitioning from a completed tackle into attacking spread
objective: Develop the ability to convert a successful tackle or forced turnover into controlled attacking spread rather than remaining congested around the original contest.
groundSize: A grid approximately 24 metres long and 20 metres wide with four outside transition gates.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
- Position two teams inside the central area.
- Mark four coloured gates around the outside.
- Begin each repetition with one team in possession.
- A coach nominates the attacking direction after a turnover.
- Legal tackles are permitted.
- A turnover may be created through a tackle, spill, intercept or pressured disposal.
- Once possession changes, the winning team must spread towards the called gate.
- Play lasts a maximum of twelve seconds after the turnover.
howTheDrillWorks:
1. One team begins with possession in the central area.
2. The defending team applies connected pressure.
3. A defender completes a legal tackle or forces a turnover.
4. The tackler releases immediately.
5. The coach calls one coloured transition gate.
6. The team winning possession spreads away from the original contest.
7. The nearest player secures the loose football.
8. Teammates provide inside, outside and backwards support.
9. The new possession team attempts to move the football through the called gate.
10. The original possession team applies counter-pressure.
11. Two points are awarded for a tackle or turnover followed by a successful exit.
12. Reset after the exit, secondary turnover or stoppage.
coachingPoints: - Complete and release the tackle before transitioning.
- Identify when possession has genuinely changed.
- The nearest player wins or secures the football.
- Other players spread away from the tackle area.
- Provide a safe first disposal.
- Avoid every player gathering around the turnover.
- Communicate the called exit gate.
- Counter-pressure immediately if the first disposal is lost.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: - Whether the tackler releases immediately.
- Whether the football is secured before players spread.
- Whether teammates create useful width and depth.
- Whether the first disposal is controlled.
- Whether congestion remains around the tackle.
- Whether the opposition applies counter-pressure.
- Whether the team maintains balance between spread and possession support.

commonErrors.error: Tackler remains attached after possession changes.| Release immediately and become a support player.
commonErrors.correction: Every player moves towards the loose football.| Allocate one ball winner and spread the remaining players.

commonErrors.error: Team attacks before securing possession.| Win the football first, then use the called exit.
commonErrors.correction: First disposal is rushed into pressure.| Use the nearest clear support option.

commonErrors.error: Players spread too far and leave the ball winner isolated.| Maintain short support before expanding fully.
commonErrors.correction: Original attacking team stops after the turnover.| Apply immediate counter-pressure.

progressions: - Remove the coach-called gate and require players to identify the best exit.
- Continue into a full scoring transition.
- Add a second turnover during the phase.
- Reduce the available transition time.
- Use match-like contact for prepared players.
regressions: - Pause after the tackle before beginning transition.
- Use pressure touches instead of tackling.
- Allow only handball after the turnover.
successIndicators: - React immediately if possession is lost again.
matchApplication: Tackles create value only when the team can secure and use the resulting possession. Rapid spread after a turnover allows defenders to become attackers before the opposition reorganises.
relatedDrills: - TK-029 – Tackle, Regain Feet and Rejoin

title: Three-Line Pressure Connection
primarySkill: Connecting pressure across defensive, midfield and forward lines
objective: Develop the connection required for pressure to transfer between team lines without leaving uncontested receivers or dangerous gaps.
groundSize: Full oval divided into forward, midfield and defensive thirds.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
- Divide the oval into three horizontal thirds.
- Position attackers and defenders in realistic match roles.
- Begin the possession team in defensive 50.
- Place one nominated pressure leader in each line.
- Players may move between thirds as the football progresses.
- Each defensive line must communicate when pressure responsibility transfers.
- Use normal match disposal rules.
- Match-like contact is used only for physically prepared players.
howTheDrillWorks:
1. The possession team attempts to move the football from defence to attack.
2. The forward line applies the first pressure on the defensive exit.
3. When possession enters the midfield third, the midfield leader calls the pressure handover.
4. Forwards recover behind the football and protect backwards options.
5. When possession enters the defensive third, defenders assume direct pressure responsibility.
6. Midfielders recover to protect the top of the defensive area.
7. The nearest balanced player in each line pressures the ball carrier.
8. Supporting players cover the next receiver and corridor space.
9. The possession team scores for reaching goal.
10. Defenders score for tackles, turnovers and forcing backwards transfers between thirds.
11. On a turnover, roles immediately reverse.
12. Play continues in blocks of three to five minutes.
coachingPoints: - Pressure must transfer before the receiver gains time.
- Each line should know when it becomes responsible.
- Previous pressure players recover behind the football.
- Protect central space during every handover.
- Maintain one direct ball-pressure player.
- Communicate receivers moving between lines.
- Avoid multiple lines chasing the same possession.
- Preserve tackle technique after long recovery runs.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: - Whether pressure handovers occur early.
- Whether each line accepts responsibility.
- Whether previous lines recover behind the football.
- Whether receivers between lines are communicated.
- Whether central gaps develop.
- Whether tackle pressure arrives before the receiver accelerates.
- Whether role reversal occurs immediately after turnovers.

commonErrors.error: Forwards continue chasing deep into midfield.| Hand pressure over and recover behind the football.
commonErrors.correction: Midfielders wait for the receiver to gain possession.| Move during the football’s flight.

commonErrors.error: Defenders step up while midfield recovery is absent.| Confirm connection before increasing pressure.
commonErrors.correction: Players between lines become unmarked.| Communicate receiver handovers early.

commonErrors.error: Several lines collapse on the football.| Keep one pressure player and preserve structure behind.
commonErrors.correction: Tackle technique deteriorates after long running.| Decelerate and restore body position before contact.

progressions: - Remove the zone lines.
- Allow unrestricted switches.
- Add scoreboard and time-pressure scenarios.
- Require player leaders to organise without coach prompts.
- Continue for longer match blocks.
regressions: - Use controlled contact instead of match-like tackling.
successIndicators: - Complete legal tackles at match speed.
matchApplication: Full-ground pressure depends on connection between forwards, midfielders and defenders. If one line fails to accept or transfer responsibility, the opposition can move through uncontested space.

title: Opposition Tactical Adjustment Game
primarySkill: Adjusting pressure systems during live play
objective: Develop the ability to recognise when the opposition changes its ball-movement method and adjust the team’s pressure system without waiting for a coach stoppage.
groundSize: Approximately three-quarters of an oval or full oval.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
- Divide players into two match-positioned teams.
- Give the possession team several hidden tactical cards.
- Tactical changes may include:
- Short uncontested possession.
- Long boundary kicking.
- Corridor handball.
- Repeated switches.
- Use of a spare behind the football.
- The defending team is not told when the attacking tactic changes.
- Nominate defensive leaders in each line.
- Match-like contact is used only for prepared players.
- Coaches do not interrupt unless safety is compromised.
howTheDrillWorks:
1. Play begins with one attacking method.
2. The defending team applies its initial pressure structure.
3. At a designated moment, the attacking captain changes the tactic.
4. Defenders observe the changed movement pattern.
5. On-field leaders identify and communicate the adjustment.
6. The pressure team changes positioning, pressing triggers or receiver priorities.
7. Legal tackles continue throughout live play.
8. The attacking team scores normally.
9. Defenders receive two points for disrupting a tactical pattern within three possessions of identifying it.
10. Defenders receive one point for forcing the attack into a less dangerous pattern.
11. Play continues for three- to five-minute blocks.
12. Review whether the adjustment was identified early enough.
coachingPoints: - Observe player positioning and disposal type, not just the football.
- Communicate when the opposition pattern changes.
- Adjust collectively rather than individually.
- Preserve core principles of ball pressure and corridor protection.
- Do not overreact to one unusual disposal.
- Confirm the pattern across several cues.
- Assign clear responsibilities after the adjustment.
- Maintain legal tackling standards during tactical change.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: - How quickly players recognise tactical change.
- Whether leaders communicate the adjustment.
- Whether all three team lines respond.
- Whether central space remains protected.
- Whether the revised pressure system affects the opposition pattern.
- Whether defenders overreact to isolated actions.
- Whether tackle roles remain clear during restructuring.

commonErrors.error: Defenders continue the original plan despite repeated opposition success.| Identify the changed pattern and adjust roles.
commonErrors.correction: One player changes position without communicating.| Make the adjustment a team call.

commonErrors.error: Defenders react to one disposal and lose structure.| Confirm the pattern before making a major tactical change.
commonErrors.correction: Tactical discussion causes ball pressure to disappear.| Maintain one immediate pressure player while leaders organise.

commonErrors.error: Players change everything at once.| Adjust the smallest number of roles required.
commonErrors.correction: Tackle discipline declines during confusion.| Preserve approach control and legal contact standards.

progressions: - Allow the opposition to change tactics multiple times.
- Remove nominated leaders.
- Add scoreboard and match-time scenarios.
- Use opponent-specific tactical patterns.
- Conduct player-led reviews between blocks.
regressions: - Use only two possible attacking patterns.
- Use controlled contact instead of match-like tackling.
successIndicators: - Maintain safe tackling during tactical change.
matchApplication: Opponents adjust during matches to escape pressure. Successful teams recognise those changes and respond on the field rather than waiting until the next quarter break.

title: Wet-Weather Tackle Pressure
primarySkill: Applying safe pressure in wet and slippery conditions
objective: Develop safe tackling and pressure behaviours when wet conditions reduce footing, ball control and the predictability of possession.
groundSize: A grid approximately 20 metres by 16 metres with one boundary side and two scoring gates.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
- Wet the footballs where conditions are dry.
- Ensure the playing surface is safe and free from dangerous slipping areas.
- Divide players into two small teams.
- Mark one boundary side and two scoring gates.
- Begin with a ground-ball or short-handball possession.
- Players must remain upright during tackle contact.
- Reduce running speed if footing becomes unsafe.
- Stop immediately if the surface creates unacceptable injury risk.
howTheDrillWorks:
1. The coach releases a wet football into the grid.
2. Players compete for possession.
3. The nearest defender applies controlled pressure.
4. Defenders use shorter approach steps to maintain footing.
5. Ball carriers may fumble or spill the football naturally.
6. Tacklers must release immediately if possession is lost.
7. Supporting defenders protect the likely ground-ball exit.
8. Teams score one point by moving the football through a gate.
9. Defenders score two points for a legal tackle or turnover and one point for forcing a boundary outcome.
10. Play continues for short blocks of 60–90 seconds.
11. Review footing, tackle height and spill reactions between blocks.
coachingPoints: - Use shorter steps and a wider base.
- Reduce closing speed earlier than in dry conditions.
- Expect the football to spill or skid.
- Keep the tackle target on the torso.
- Avoid diving or sliding into the opponent’s legs.
- Release immediately when possession is lost.
- Use the boundary and body position to reduce movement options.
- Prioritise safety if footing deteriorates.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: - Whether players maintain footing.
- Whether approach speed is adjusted.
- Whether tackle height stays legal.
- Whether players avoid sliding contact.
- Whether tacklers release after spills.
- Whether supporting defenders react to unpredictable football movement.
- Whether the drill remains safe for the surface conditions.

commonErrors.error: Defender approaches with long uncontrolled strides.| Shorten the steps and lower the centre of gravity.
commonErrors.correction: Player slides into the opponent’s legs.| Stay upright and reduce speed earlier.

commonErrors.error: Tackler continues holding after a fumble.| Release immediately and contest the loose football.
commonErrors.correction: Defender watches the wet football and loses the opponent.| Track the torso and hips.

commonErrors.error: Players attempt dry-weather disposal and movement speed.| Simplify decisions and control the pace.
commonErrors.correction: Drill continues on an unsafe surface.| Stop or modify the activity immediately.

progressions: - Add repeated ground-ball contests.
- Allow short kicks with a wet football.
- Introduce boundary throw-in pressure.
- Continue into a small-sided wet-weather game.
- Add a time limit for disposal.
regressions: - Use damp rather than fully wet footballs.
- Use pressure touches instead of tackles.
successIndicators: - Use simple and effective pressure decisions.
matchApplication: Wet football increases fumbles, ground contests and uncontrolled movement. Players must reduce approach speed, remain upright and react immediately when possession becomes loose.

title: Fatigue Decision Pressure Circuit
primarySkill: Maintaining pressure decisions under football-specific fatigue
objective: Assess and develop the ability to select the correct pressure action while physically fatigued without compromising legal tackling technique.
groundSize: Five stations occupying approximately one-third of an oval.
equipment: - Heart-rate or work-time monitor where available
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
- Construct five connected stations:
- Acceleration and deceleration.
- Live corral-or-tackle decision.
- Smother-or-tackle decision.
- Recovery chase.
- Two-player pressure rotation.
- Players complete one action at each station before moving immediately to the next.
- Work periods last 30–45 seconds.
- Provide full recovery between sets.
- Coaches monitor technique and stop unsafe repetitions.
- Match players appropriately for contact stations.
howTheDrillWorks:
1. Players begin with a short acceleration and deceleration effort.
2. At Station 2, the attacker either enters tackle range or remains evasive.
3. The defender selects tackle or corral.
4. At Station 3, the ball carrier prepares to dispose or retains possession.
5. The defender selects smother pressure or a legal tackle.
6. At Station 4, the defender completes a recovery chase to a side-on pressure position.
7. At Station 5, two defenders rotate pressure against two attackers.
8. Coaches score each decision and technical action.
9. Players receive one point for the correct decision and one point for safe execution.
10. Any unsafe contact ends the player’s set.
11. Complete two to four sets per player.
coachingPoints: - Fatigue does not justify poor tackle technique.
- Decelerate before every contact decision.
- Corral when safe tackle range is absent.
- Smother when disposal is already committed.
- Maintain legal tackle height.
- Communicate during two-player pressure.
- Stop the set if head position or body control deteriorates.
- Prioritise quality over completion speed.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: - Whether decision accuracy declines under fatigue.
- Whether deceleration becomes less effective.
- Whether tackle height rises.
- Whether players choose desperate contact.
- Whether communication declines.
- Whether recovery effort remains controlled.
- Whether coaches intervene when safety standards fall.

commonErrors.error: Player treats every station as a tackle opportunity.| Read the situation and select corral or smother when appropriate.
commonErrors.correction: Deceleration disappears late in the set.| Reduce speed earlier or end the repetition.

commonErrors.error: Tackler’s head moves in front of the opponent.| Restore side-on entry and reduce closing speed.
commonErrors.correction: Player reaches because of fatigue.| Continue moving the feet or choose containment.

commonErrors.error: Communication stops at the final station.| Require clear pressure and support calls.
commonErrors.correction: Player prioritises circuit speed over safety.| Score technical quality more heavily than completion time.

progressions: - Reduce recovery between sets.
- Randomise the station order.
- Add scoreboard consequences.
- Increase live attacking freedom.
- Complete the circuit before a short match-simulation block.
regressions: - Use tackle bags rather than live opponents.
- Replace live tackles with pressure touches.
successIndicators: - Make correct pressure decisions while fatigued.
- Maintain safe tackle height and head position.
matchApplication: Late in quarters and during repeat contests, fatigue affects judgement as well as movement. Players must continue selecting the correct defensive action instead of relying on desperate tackle attempts.

title: Free-Kick Risk Pressure Management
primarySkill: Applying pressure without conceding avoidable free kicks
objective: Develop disciplined pressure that influences the opponent while avoiding high, low, late, in-the-back or protected-area infringements.
groundSize: A grid approximately 24 metres by 18 metres with four scenario zones.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
- Divide the grid into four scenario zones:
- Receiver after a mark.
- Ball carrier preparing to dispose.
- Ground-ball collector.
- Boundary-side ball carrier.
- Position attackers and defenders at each zone.
- Coaches act as umpires and clearly signal outcomes.
- Defenders score for effective legal pressure.
- Attackers score for clean exits or free kicks.
- Rotate players every three to four minutes.
- Contact remains controlled.
howTheDrillWorks:
1. At the mark zone, the defender establishes a legal position and reacts to play on.
2. At the disposal zone, the defender pressures without making late contact.
3. At the ground-ball zone, the defender protects the player with their head over the football.
4. At the boundary zone, the defender corrals without driving the opponent over the line.
5. Coaches award two points for a legal tackle or turnover.
6. One point is awarded for pressure that forces a poor disposal.
7. The attacker receives two points for an avoidable defensive free kick.
8. Players must explain the pressure decision after selected repetitions.
9. Rotate through every scenario.
10. Finish with a short game in which free-kick discipline affects the score.
coachingPoints: - Pressure is valuable only when it remains legal.
- Respect marks and protected areas.
- Avoid contact after clean disposal.
- Protect the player whose head is over the football.
- Move beside a rear-quarter opponent before tackling.
- Corral near the boundary rather than driving through the player.
- Release immediately when possession is lost.
- Understand when not tackling is the best defensive decision.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: - Whether players understand the different risk scenarios.
- Whether approach speed is controlled.
- Whether contact timing is legal.
- Whether protected areas are respected.
- Whether vulnerable players are protected.
- Whether defenders choose containment when tackling is unsafe.
- Whether repeated infringements reveal a technical or decision issue.

commonErrors.error: Defender contacts after disposal.| Stop the tackle action once the football is cleanly released.
commonErrors.correction: Player enters the protected area.| Hold the legal mark position until play on.

commonErrors.error: Tackler contacts a player over the football.| Control the exit and wait until the player rises.
commonErrors.correction: Defender drives directly through the back.| Reach a side-on position before contact.

commonErrors.error: Tackler forces the opponent across the boundary.| Secure the tackle and stop applying force.
commonErrors.correction: Player believes pressure requires contact.| Use corralling, smothering and receiver denial when tackling is unsafe.

progressions: - Combine all scenarios in a continuous small-sided game.
- Add scoreboard and red-time context.
- Use player umpires to explain decisions.
- Increase attacker freedom.
- Apply match-like contact for prepared senior groups.
regressions: - Use pressure touches rather than tackles.
